entries.title: Trump Administration Says Taxpayer-Funded Ads Suit Should End With the Midterms
entries.summary: The Justice Department argued that the lawsuit is irrelevant now that Election Day is over — and that the challengers’ claims of harm never came to pass.
entries.content:
The Trump administration says a lawsuit over its taxpayer-funded advertising campaign should be considered moot now that the midterm elections are over, arguing that a judge can no longer remedy any harm the ads might have caused.

Government lawyers want U.S. District Judge Jennifer L. Rochon to reconsider nonprofit Common Cause’s request to block a series of government ads because the midterms have already concluded, saying the “injuries” mentioned in the nonprofit’s suit never materialized before or after Election Day.

“Plaintiffs cannot establish any ‘actual and imminent’ harms related to the 2026 midterms because those elections have concluded, and their alleged post-midterm harms are plainly remote and speculative,” the Thursday filing says, adding that “the relief they seek will not redress their alleged harm.”

The dispute stems from revelations reported in September that U.S. Customs and Border Protection awarded a $20 million contract for a national media campaign to air ads with pro-Trump political messaging, including one spot that promised Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans won control of Congress.

President Donald Trump announced in October that he would pay for the ads himself and with money raised through his super PAC, MAGA Inc., though the White House later confirmed that he would not reimburse the government for earlier ad spending.

Last week, the court froze the media contract through Nov. 20 and blocked the administration from airing three “purely partisan” midterm ads on official websites and commercial spots through Nov. 13. Ahead of that decision, Rochon said she was “hard pressed” to see how the tax-funded messages could be considered anything other than a direct pitch to voters to support Republicans on Tuesday’s ballot.

Common Cause and Alabama state legislative candidate Robert Hunter allege the government used public resources to benefit Trump’s political allies, saying the ads could still hurt their political activities in future elections. The challengers said in a Monday motion that the court should grant a longer-term freeze on the broadcast spots.

Government lawyers on Thursday dismissed those concerns as speculative and irrelevant now that Election Day has passed.

The Justice Department defended White House employees’ work compiling ad videos, saying they received their regular salaries without the need for additional staff spending, and thus “no diversion of appropriated funds,” Assistant U.S. Attorney Jeffrey Oestericher wrote.

The filing also backed the government’s promotion of potential $5,000 checks, saying the ad informed “the general public of a new monetary proposal as well as the Administration’s views on tax policy.”

entries.title: Federal Judge Quickly Blocks Construction on Trump’s Arch After Panel Approval
entries.summary: The National Capital Planning Commission, stacked with Trump allies, gave the plans final approval hours before the judge's ruling.
entries.content:
A federal judge blocked construction on President Donald Trump's monumental arch late Thursday evening, about two hours after the project had received final approval from a federal panel.

The National Capital Planning Commission, stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 in favor of the 250-foot arch set to be built at Memorial Circle on the west end of Arlington Memorial Bridge, despite overwhelming public opposition to the project.

U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a restraining order pausing construction on the arch for 14 days, ruling in favor of local jurisdictions and veterans who challenged the arch’s legality.

Lawsuits filed by three Vietnam War veterans, Arlington County officials and D.C. and Virginia’s attorneys general seek to block the arch, arguing it doesn't have proper congressional approval, will impede Arlington National Cemetery and create environmental and safety issues.

Construction would have begun once the Interior Department issued work authorization and the National Park Service published notice — rubber stamps that the administration said it wanted to occur immediately — had Chutkan not blocked the project.

The government is prohibited from “initiating, making, or otherwise effectuating any construction, excavation, demolition, land-disturbance, utility-installation, or roadway-closure activity, or any other construction-related activity at or near Memorial Circle in Washington, D.C., that is for the purpose of constructing an arch at Memorial Circle,” the judge’s order says.

Chutkan, a Barack Obama appointee, ordered the government to file a status report by Monday to certify their compliance with the order and to ensure all employees and contractors pause construction activities.

Earlier Thursday, the planning commission hosted its meeting virtually to accommodate massive public interest. Hundreds of people, from Maryland to Michigan, tuned in to watch, and 131 people signed up to speak during public comment. The livestream crashed about an hour into the hearing, when just four people had given their testimony. The video restarted after 30 minutes.

“President Trump's exceptional leadership has made Washington, D.C., a city worthy of its capital name. He has renovated the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, cleaned up countless statues and fountains,” Mark Paoletta, chair of the National Capital Planning Commission and White House official, said at Thursday’s meeting. “President Trump understands, as president and a superb builder, that it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments.”

Between insulting commissioners for caving to Trump’s wishes and dogging the arch as a “new toy” and a “personal vanity project,” members of the public asked the panel to “look within your heart” and reject the proposal.

Trump arch Veteran Protest (5599x3733, AR: 1.50)
Michael Lemmon, the lead plaintiff in the veterans’ lawsuit, was one of the first to speak and asked the commission to strike down Trump’s monument. Earlier Thursday, before the vote, he stood behind the Lincoln Memorial and looked out across the river at Arlington National Cemetery. Speaking to members of the press, he said the view brings him peace he didn’t often know as a veteran of one of the nation’s most divisive conflicts, and Trump’s arch will take that away.

“I have a duty as a Vietnam vet, as a survivor, to my buddies buried there to honor their sacrifice and protect their memories,” Lemmon said, choking back tears. “The arch would profoundly disturb the peace and tranquility owed them by towering over the dead. … It is frankly blasphemous.”

His testimony echoed the concerns of historic preservationists who worry the arch will limit the historic view corridor that connects Arlington and D.C.

Paoletta said Trump’s arch will fulfill a congressionally approved 1925 plan to erect two slender columns at the end of Arlington Memorial Bridge. The current design of the bridge “dishonors our veterans and leaves a key monumental gateway to Arlington that Congress authorized incomplete,” Paoletta said. “This is a national disgrace.”

The administration has relied on that 1925 plan as justification for the arch’s design, despite his monument clocking in 84 feet taller than the century-old plan. It also touts the arch’s location and stature as an opportunity to act as a military defense complex, housing drone defense systems to protect national security. The plans voted on by the planning commission omit any military infrastructure details.

arch/IMG_9938 copy.jpg (4032x2688, AR: 1.50)
At the same time Lemmon spoke on the steps behind the Lincoln Memorial, protestors just across the Potomac River near the monument’s planned construction site raised their own bamboo version of Trump’s arch, with a stark red “X” on each side.

Among them, in a yellow safety vest, stood Ralph Nix, a retired Navy veteran who served for 20 years. He called the arch a disgrace not only to veterans, but also to their families.

“The last thing I feel is that an arch to the most corrupt president of the United States needs to be in front of the most sacred ground of people who have lost their lives to defend this country. This guy, he does not deserve it,” Nix said. “He has disgraced the military. He’s spending hundreds of millions of dollars on this arch while at the same time taking away benefits from the veterans.”

The final cost of Trump’s arch is unknown, but estimates place the price at $100 million. It is expected to bring anywhere from 2,000 to 22,000 visitors daily, according to estimates from the administration.

Commissioner Kevin Lilly, an assistant secretary with the Interior Department, said at the beginning of the meeting he would cast his vote not only as a public servant, but as a veteran — and someone with loved ones buried in Arlington cemetery. He said the arch will not take away from the hallowed grounds of the cemetery or act as distraction, but instead will be a tribute to the 430,000 people buried there.

“This arch does not represent partisanship or politics,” Lilly said. “It stands for the courage of those who served, the sacrifices of those who never came home, and, in a greater sense, the triumph of the American spirit and the enduring strength of a nation made possible by sacrifice, commitment, and a faith in God's providence over our great land.”

This story was updated to reflect Chutkan's later ruling.

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: ‘A Tsunami of Change’
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro Newsletter for Nov. 5, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

 In today’s newsletter: The future of feds in D.C., Metro service cuts and the Chesapeake Bay Bridge. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 6/10. A damp, foggy start may give way to some afternoon sunshine in spots. Mild temperatures are a plus, with highs in the 60s to around 70. Read the full forecast.





THE LATEST

“A tsunami of change is coming to our city and to the U.S. Capitol,” D.C. Council member Brooke Pinto declared at the start of a Thursday hearing.

Perhaps most immediately, five Republican-helmed states that sent National Guard troops to support President Donald Trump’s “safe and beautiful” task force in D.C. now have Democratic governors who could (in theory) recall those troops come January.

Pinto called on those governors to do so in a hearing focused on increasing transparency for federal agents policing D.C., The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports.

Dozens of activists and city residents attending the hearings expressed deep concern with what they described as a lack of action from local officials to push back against the Trump administration’s law enforcement presence in their neighborhoods.

The administration has shown no signs of retreat. Politico reported yesterday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has authorized the D.C. Guard to start using marked police cars, humvees, “light medium tactical vehicles” and … boats.

The boats are to conduct “perimeter security” for police in Anacostia and help federal agents arrest suspects who try to evade law enforcement by jumping into the river. As you do.

Pinto called it “the exact opposite of the approach that we need to be taking.”

“I am disturbed to see this administration continue to act in a way that is not supporting safety in the District … and that feels very un-American,” she said.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. isn’t a state, but could the city’s wards be treated the same as counties?

It’s not exactly a question you’d debate at a dinner party, but it sits at the heart of a clever yet untested ploy by D.C. officials to blunt the impact of new federal work requirements for Medicaid recipients.

D.C. has asked the federal government for a hardship waiver to the work requirements, which go into effect in January. The city is relying on a provision of the law that allows states to request the waiver for counties where the unemployment rate is above 8%.

Now, D.C. doesn’t have any counties, and the city’s overall unemployment rate is 5.6%. But The Sun’s Martin Austermuhle reports that officials have applied for the waiver just for wards 7 and 8, where the unemployment rate is 9.5% and 10%, respectively.

There are 75,000 Medicaid-eligible D.C. residents who could be subject to the new work requirements, and roughly 30,000 of them live in wards 7 and 8.

“Our primary concern is ensuring that residents do not unnecessarily lose Medicaid coverage because of barriers to meeting or documenting work requirements, particularly in communities where employment opportunities are more limited,” said Wayne Turnage, D.C.’s deputy mayor for health and human services.

The move has made at least one lawmaker “uneasy.” At-Large council member Christina Henderson says “it’s not that someone’s ward is why they can’t find work.” She’s also worried about the city’s broader outreach to Medicaid recipients about the new work requirements, telling The Sun that she thinks D.C. is “woefully unprepared.”





FROM THE DISTRICT

Metro cuts en route? During Thursday’s WMATA board meeting, General Manager Randy Clarke indicated that the agency’s upcoming budget will “very likely” include service cuts due to a lack of funding. The Sun’s Will Hofmann reports that Clarke did not mention specific cuts, but noted how they might affect the system.

“[They would] further reduce on-time performance, crowding is going to go up on our bus system, routes are going to take longer and we are going to drop more trips,” Clarke said, adding that “we don’t have the funding to continue the current service we are providing.”

Special education in D.C. is in “crisis,” parents and teachers told the council this week in two hearings, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. There is a stark achievement gap between students with disabilities and the general student body, exacerbated by special education bus issues and overcrowded classrooms.

Foie gras may have fallen afowl with voters this week, but the fight to ban the delicacy in the District isn’t over yet, Will reports. Questions remain about how the ban will be enforced, and a foie gras producer plans to take legal action against it.

The D.C. Preservation League asked a federal court on Thursday to enter a 14-day temporary restraining order against the Trump administration from closing East Potomac Golf Links by Nov. 15, The Sun’s Justice Covert reports.

We’ve got a proper D.C. Council seat standoff. The D.C. Democratic Party confirmed on Thursday evening that it has appointed Jamal Holtz to serve as an interim at-large council member to fill the seat vacated by Robert White earlier this week. The only issue? Current At-Large council member Christina Henderson has similarly made a play for that seat, as we reported earlier this week. How will this all end? It’s still unclear.




FROM VIRGINIA

Public hearings on the proposed $67 billion merger between Dominion Energy and NextEra Energy began this week at the State Corporation Commission. The deal, which would create the world’s largest regulated utility, has been strongly opposed by lawmakers, consumer advocates and citizens in the months leading up to the hearings, The Virginia Mercury reports.





FROM MARYLANDBuilding bridges: Federal highway officials have signed off on the environmental review process for replacing the Chesapeake Bay Bridge, a major step in an infrastructure project that could cost up to $17.6 billion, The Banner reports. Construction could start as soon as 2032.





METRO MOMENT

Olivia the duck foie gras ban (5867x3911, AR: 1.50)
The biggest winner of Election Day in D.C.? Olivia the duck.

The mascot of a campaign to ban foie gras, she made a grand entrance into Solly’s in Shaw on Tuesday night for a watch party. With small golden duck ornaments scattered across tables as decoration, partygoers munched on vegan sliders and pizza as Olivia quacked away in one corner, drawing a crowd.

As it became clear the ban would pass, she was taken downstairs, where supporters were showering each other with champagne. Just outside of the splash zone, Olivia flapped her wings with (seeming) delight.





SPORTS

The Spirit hopes to kick off another playoff run this weekend when it hosts the Portland Thorns in the NWSL quarterfinals. The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri has everything you need to know ahead of the postseason.

Commanders corner Trey Amos is no savior, but his return is a major boost for Washington’s inconsistent defense. After missing almost a year with injuries, the second-year player is back on the field and trying to take things just one snap at a time, The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson reports.

Ever heard of the fair catch free kick rule in football? If not, you’re certainly not alone. But at Division III Johns Hopkins, the staff and players were well aware of the odd wrinkle last Saturday, when they used it to beat Muhlenberg College in the final seconds, The Sun’s Jesse Dougherty writes. Read this and you’ll be ready to coach special teams in no time.

What to Watch This Weekend

Friday

NBA: Wizards at Hawks, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

Saturday

NHL: Capitals vs. Panthers, 12:30 p.m. (Monumental)

NCAAF: Maryland at Purdue, 12:30 p.m. (BTN)

MLS: D.C. United vs. New York City FC, 4 p.m. (Apple TV)

NCAAM: Maryland at Georgetown, 7:30 p.m. (Peacock)

NBA: Wizards at Thunder, 8 p.m. (Monumental)

Sunday

NFL: Commanders vs. Rams, 1 p.m. (Fox 5)

NCAAW: Maryland vs. George Mason, 1 p.m. (B1G+)

NWSL: Spirit vs. Portland Thorns, 3 p.m. (ABC)

NFL: Buccaneers at Bears, 8:20 p.m. (NBC)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

entries.title: Jay Rockefeller, a Giant of West Virginia Politics, Dies at 89
entries.summary: Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states.
entries.content:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family’s political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia’s governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.

Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller’s wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.

Rockefeller came from one of the nation’s richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.

“I could not imagine a more rewarding career,” Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.

He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller’s birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.

Jay Rockefeller went in a different direction.

A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.

“It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles,” he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.

While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family’s Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.

A turning point came after Rockefeller’s only political defeat in the 1972 governor’s race to Republican Arch A. Moore Jr., whose daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, was elected in 2014 to Rockefeller’s Senate seat upon his retirement.

After the defeat, Rockefeller remained in West Virginia, a decision he called the most important of his career. He became the first without a theological degree to become president of West Virginia Wesleyan College in 1973. His popularity there — and a change in his stance to embrace strip mining — translated to a landslide win over Republican Cecil Underwood in the 1976 governor’s race.

As governor, Rockefeller emphasized development of the state’s infrastructure, such as roads, sewers and bridges. Those issues, he said, are “not very sexy things, I grant you but very, very necessary in West Virginia.”

After Rockefeller defeated Arch Moore in a rematch in 1980, he won a U.S. Senate seat in 1984 after the retirement of longtime Democrat Jennings Randolph. It came despite a landslide victory that year for Republican President Ronald Reagan.

Rockefeller and his wife, Sharon, daughter of former Republican Sen. Charles Percy of Illinois, fit easily into the capital’s social scene, purchasing a multimillion-dollar estate for their family. Never shy or apologetic about using his inherited $150 million fortune to win his races, he spent millions upon millions from his own pocket. He won by comfortable margins in each of his five terms.

Rockefeller’s vast wealth was always a source of conversation and an undercurrent in his political races. He spent at least $21 million of his own money in his political campaigns, including $9 million to win a close 1984 Senate race against Republican novice and fellow multimillionaire John Raese. In Rockefeller’s 1980 gubernatorial race against Republican Arch Moore Jr., bumper stickers appeared saying: “Make Him Spend It All, Arch.”

The state’s junior senator for 25 years, Rockefeller carved his own path of influence in Sen. Robert C. Byrd’s immense shadow. Byrd died in 2010 as the longest-serving senator in U.S. history, winning an enduring reputation for steering billions of dollars over many decades to boost his impoverished state.

Rockefeller’s influence was less showy. As chairman of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, he championed consumers’ rights, upgrading broadband infrastructure and sponsoring a bill to block companies from tracking online activity of their customers. He authored legislation in 1997 that created the Children’s Health Insurance Program, which assists poor families whose incomes are too high to qualify for Medicaid.

He also was head of committees on Veterans Affairs and Intelligence, frequently sparring with President George W. Bush over foreign policy. Rockefeller said he regretted his 2002 vote to authorize the war against Iraq.

But Rockefeller also differed with the Democratic administration of President Barack Obama over mining-related regulations. With his state the nation’s second-biggest coal producer, Rockefeller was among several West Virginia officials who opposed the Obama-era Environmental Protection Agency’s oversight of the mountaintop removal method of surface mining.

College studies in Tokyo laid the groundwork for Rockefeller’s efforts to bring business from Japan to West Virginia. He had known Toyota’s founding family since the 1960s and was instrumental in helping the Japanese automaker pick a Buffalo, West Virginia, cornfield for an engine parts plant in 1996. The $2 billion plant now employs about 2,200 workers.

entries.title: Jordan Smith Jr. Returns to the DMV as a Highly Touted NBA Prospect
entries.summary: The Paul VI product and his new teammates at Arkansas will face Virginia at Capital One Arena on Sunday.
entries.content:
As a self-proclaimed “die-hard Wizards fan,” Jordan Smith Jr. has attended many games at Capital One Arena in his life. But he’s never had the chance to walk on to the court, let alone play on it.

That changes this weekend, as Smith — who made a name for himself as a top high school player for Paul VI in Chantilly, Virginia — returns to the DMV on Sunday as a member of the No. 12 Arkansas Razorbacks to take on the No. 9 Virginia Cavaliers in the Capital Showcase.

The 19-year-old D.C. native said he’s excited to play in front of friends and family on the same court once shared by his childhood idols, something he considers a “dream come true.”

“You know, after watching John Wall, Bradley Beal, those guys, I’m just really happy to be able to go home and play on the Wizards’ floor,” Smith said. “Not a lot of people can say they’ve done that, and just for me, I’m a big D.C. guy, big Wizards guy. I’m just excited.”

Sunday’s contest against Virginia will be Smith’s second-ever college start after a dazzling debut over Arkansas-Pine Bluff earlier this week. The 6-foot-2 guard recorded 20 points, four rebounds and two assists in the Razorbacks’ 106-61 win — a performance that helped boost his soaring draft stock.

In a recent ranking of 2027 NBA Draft prospects by ESPN, Smith was listed at No. 4. But the freshman said that none of that hype means much to him.

“It’s good to have that recognition, but there’s always more work to do,” Smith said. “Just don’t let your head fall in love with it. It’s really just a target on your back. Everyone’s coming after you every game.”

Smith said he’ll be sure to give his teammates a proper tour of the District this weekend. Personally, he plans on visiting Ben's Chili Bowl and his dad’s rec center, where he often played as a kid.

Outside of the homecoming, though, this is a business trip for Smith and the Razorbacks. While his first college start was another “dream come true,” Smith made clear that his mindset has already changed to “kill mode” against the top-10 Cavaliers.

“The exhibition games were kind of, for me, just to get my footing right,” Smith said. “But now, ever since the first game, my mentality has been different. Just kill or be killed, because the season relies on these types of games just to see where we’re at.”

entries.title: How Stephen Miller’s Fixation on Minnesota’s Somalis Became a Full-Scale Crackdown
entries.summary: The new White House chief of staff has spent the last year moving the federal government against one community in one state.
entries.content:
Stephen Miller was on a quest.

The president’s fierce loyalist, at the time his deputy chief of staff, pressed administration officials for evidence of fraud related to immigrants, Minnesota and the state’s Somali population nine times in a span of about 10 minutes during a December 2025 call, according to a recording obtained by The Washington Sun.

Miller cut one official off as they were describing a fraud problem in Florida, a hot spot for bad actors who siphon off government benefits, according to the government’s own data. He appeared uninterested in the official’s description of fraud when it didn’t prominently feature immigrants.

At one point, Miller was told about an active criminal investigation into a national fraud case out of the Eastern District of Virginia.

“I hear you, but that’s a long way off from Minneapolis,” Miller responded.

The call is one of several previously unreported instances since the fall of 2025 in which Miller pushed administration officials to target a small population of immigrants in a single state. A White House official told The Sun in a statement that the call “was focused on rooting out fraud in Minnesota” and that there is “no denying the Somali population was a large part of the massive fraud in the state.”

Miller has repeatedly sought to wield the full weight of the federal government against the roughly 100,000 Somalis who live in Minnesota, targeting the state’s federal funds, installing an ally of his immigration agenda in a key position at the Justice Department and clashing with career and political officials in the process.

“It’s like a passion project for him,” one source close to the White House said.

Miller has only strengthened his power in the aftermath of a brutal election for his party. On Friday, President Donald Trump named Miller his chief of staff — a personal achievement for Miller that makes explicit his long-standing dominion over the president’s domestic agenda.

Miller’s fraud push emerged in the aftermath of a major scandal over fraudulent payments in Minnesota, in which a disproportionate number of people of Somali descent were charged with pilfering hundreds of millions from government programs. Miller’s offensive has had its own seismic impact.

The administration sent thousands of federal officers to the state for immigration enforcement, a surge that resulted in two Americans being killed by federal agents. It froze hundreds of millions in Medicaid funding and threatened millions more in child care and food stamp programs.

Mosques and day cares in Minneapolis have been forced to hire additional security in response to a demonization campaign accelerated by the federal government. The funding cuts threaten instability for millions of state residents of all ethnic backgrounds.

“We have literally seen a full government response to attack the community on the ground through propaganda, economic sanctions and the invasion of one state as if we were a hostile territory that had to be dominated,” said Doran Schrantz, a board member and former director of Faith In Minnesota, a grassroots nonprofit.
Immigration Minnesota AP-26008609255769 (2591x1728, AR: 1.50)Miller’s focus on the Somali population in Minnesota has frustrated some in the administration who have sought a more holistic approach to rooting out fraud, two administration officials told The Sun.

The focus “was not necessarily fraud writ large,” but on “the specific population of immigrants,” one of those officials said, calling the campaign “inane.”

Miller, newly empowered, is under intense pressure from his right to to do even more to go after Somalis in Minnesota.

“Miller is pushing this fraud stuff desperately to get his reputation back on the right because he’s getting hammered for being a sellout who did nothing,” one former Trump aide said. “There’s been no mass deportations. This is all brand salvaging from him.”

In a statement to The Sun, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said, “President Trump has launched an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government, holding criminals accountable and saving taxpayers billions of dollars. This administration has a zero-tolerance policy for anyone who steals from the American taxpayer.”

How Miller directed a government crackdown on Minnesota

Miller’s directives on fraud in Minnesota reached at least five federal agencies in the last year, attempting to touch everything from how Somalis and other Minnesotans receive access to nutrition assistance and health services to how they send money to their families.

In the fall of 2025, Miller pushed Treasury officials to scrutinize bank reports generated in Minnesota in an attempt to identify transfers of ill-gotten money out of the U.S.

Treasury aides, including Trump appointees, pushed back: The action Miller was seeking wouldn’t capture what he said he wanted, which was anything suspicious between government agencies and Somali-run private nonprofits, two sources with direct knowledge of the conversations said.

Miller pressed Treasury officials to find other ways to use the financial system to crack down on Somali immigrants. In response to the pressure, Treasury implemented an order requiring financial firms in two Minnesota counties to report all international transactions over $3,000.

Treasury staff was concerned that doing so violated constitutional protections against overly broad law enforcement searches, the two sources said. Somali businesses have said the federal action has created a panic about their ability to send money home. In internal conversations, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been supportive of aggressively using financial tools to root out fraud, one source said.

Administration officials were especially taken by a Nov. 29, 2025, New York Times article about Minnesota’s fraud crisis, concluding they needed to mount “a strong public response,” one source familiar with the fraud work told The Sun.

Around that time, the administration issued a barrage of threats against Minnesota, some at Miller’s request.

Miller’s team pushed top political officials multiple times to cut up to $150 million in Department of Agriculture funding to the state late last year and early this year, including food assistance, according to an administration official.
AP26303679383536 (4007x2837, AR: 1.41)The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told Minnesota in early December to submit a plan by January to combat Medicaid fraud or risk losing funding. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins did similarly just over a week later, demanding Minnesota recertify the over 100,000 Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program participants in four counties in and around Minneapolis in only 30 days — a process that includes in-person interviews — or face administrative funding cuts. (A judge later blocked Rollins’ demand.)

The administration’s actions toward Minnesota went into hyperdrive after conservative YouTuber Nick Shirley published a viral video on Dec. 26 in which he visited Minnesota day cares, purporting to uncover fraud. Within weeks, Trump established a new fraud division within the Justice Department, CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz informed Minnesota of his intention to withhold up to $2 billion in annual Medicaid funding, and Rollins announced on X that her department was freezing nearly $130 million in funding to Minnesota, and specifically to Minneapolis.

The Administration for Children and Families, too, froze federal funds for child care services to Minnesota and four other states.

While ACF has authority to address suspected fraud, it bypassed its own process, said Ruth Friedman, who directed the office of child care at ACF under the Biden administration. The letters to states “were extraordinarily unusual and did not follow established procedure and regulation,” she said. Courts quickly blocked the freezes and ACF later walked them back.

The administration partially justified its immigration enforcement surge in the state by pointing to the growing fraud scandal. The surge exploded into national outrage in January, when federal agents killed two U.S. citizens, Renée Good and Alex Pretti.

The political outcry over the killings, including from some Republicans, led the White House to lessen its physical law enforcement presence in the state. But at least one of Miller’s allies in the law enforcement surge would go on to become a key figure in the fraud fight.

Miller and the administration, the source close to the White House said, viewed going after fraud in immigrant communities as a “more politically opportune way to highlight the issue with immigration rather than ramping up enforcement in the same graphic way.”

In his State of the Union address, Trump announced that Vice President JD Vance would be leading a “war on fraud” and cited “Somali pirates.” Days later, Vance announced that the government was freezing nearly $260 million in Medicaid funding to Minnesota. The anti-fraud task force was formalized in March, with Vance in charge and Miller as a senior advisor.

One month later, the Justice Department swore in Colin McDonald as its first ever assistant attorney general to lead the new fraud enforcement division. Ever since, he has been Miller’s “top lieutenant” within the Justice Department, according to a senior administration official.

“He’s basically doing Miller’s bidding,” the official said.

Miller maintains a direct pipeline to McDonald, a relationship they previously established when the assistant attorney general was Miller’s point person within the DOJ on immigration. That included the administration deporting Venezuelans without due process under the Alien Enemies Act, as well as law enforcement surges in Minneapolis and other U.S. cities.

Because Miller saw the fraud work as nearly singularly focused on immigration, the senior administration official said, McDonald became a natural fit to lead the Justice Department’s new push. Miller now turns to McDonald for any issue related to fraud.

“For fraud, Somali fraud in Minnesota was his biggest target,” the official said of Miller.

The DOJ did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the Treasury Department said in a statement that “the entire administration is completely united in rooting out waste, fraud and abuse.” HHS declined to comment. The Agriculture Department said fraud has been a priority from Day One of Trump’s presidency and did not respond to a request for comment on Miller’s role.

Fraud as an immigration issue

In the backdrop of Miller’s focus on Minnesota and the immigrant population is a real fraud problem in government programs that worsened during the pandemic. The Government Accountability Office estimates the government loses $233 billion to $521 billion every year to fraud.

In Minnesota, the sprawling fraud scandal across the state’s social services programs included one nonprofit, Feeding Our Future, fraudulently obtaining and dispersing $250 million in federal funds, according to the Justice Department.

By the end of last December, almost 100 people had been charged with schemes to defraud social safety net programs meant to treat children with autism, feed children and house vulnerable Minnesotans with disabilities. More than 80 of those charged were people of Somali descent.

Many in the Trump administration came into office intent on culling back what they saw as government programs drowning in waste after the pandemic. That work remains underway, and in some corners of the federal government, officials feel they’ve made progress — in part due to the top-down pressure from the White House.

Several administration officials say Miller’s focus has been more narrow. Fraud, in Miller’s telling, is an immigration issue.

“If you're a middle-class taxpayer in this country, before President Trump came along, you spent half your working life paying for fraudsters and scammers, many of whom are refugees, illegal aliens and foreigners who came to this country to loot and plunder us,” Miller told the press during the launch of a new fraud tip line in October.
Trump AP-26218734245261 (5059x3372, AR: 1.50)Miller’s extreme messaging has shut out some who may have been natural allies in anti-fraud efforts.

“There is an actual fraud problem here. It's just not a fraud problem related to immigration, and it’s not even a fraud problem related primarily to individual beneficiaries,” said Linda Miller, president of the Program Integrity Alliance who worked at the Government Accountability Office on fraud for a decade. “It's a much bigger, more systematic problem.”

The leader of a security-focused trade group heavily focused on reducing fraud, granted anonymity to speak freely, told The Sun that the group’s members don’t want to work with the White House because of the rhetoric.

“You have to have some really screwed up messaging when a coalition of companies — most of whom are dedicated to fighting fraud — are reticent to engage with a White House that’s trying to do more on it,” they said, “because the way that they have framed it has made the politics so toxic that they’d rather just stay away.”

In an interview with The Sun, Oz said Miller was not as involved as other task force members in the nuts and bolts of addressing chronic fraud in government health care programs.

Miller’s rhetoric, Oz said, is “not frustrating at all” and highlights “something all of us need to acknowledge.”

“We built our social infrastructure, our safety net system in a high-trust society,” Oz said. “If you allow our communities to become so corrupt that everyone expects there to be people stealing from the poor, that’s a massive problem for the country.”

Pressure from the right is growing

To Liam Donovan, a longtime Republican strategist, the focus on Minnesota was as an effort to reconstitute the best moment of the election cycle for Republicans: After Shirley’s YouTube video about fraud went viral, but before federal agents shot and killed American citizens.

The administration has been “looking for another Nick Shirley moment,” Donovan said.

That was “political bliss,” he said.

Miller is now facing a very different environment in the face of overwhelming Democratic wins in the midterms. The Republican party is facing a reckoning from the left, but Miller, at the center of Trump’s agenda, is still facing pressure from the right.

Ryan James Girdusky, founder of the right-wing 1776 Project PAC, praised Miller and noted he was constrained by the legal obstacles that make it difficult to deport Somalian immigrants, who are largely here legally. But Gidursky also acknowledged Miller was under pressure from the right to carry out more aggressive actions. “Some people always want more.”

Gregory Bovino, former top official at Customs and Border Patrol who left the administration after intense fallout from the fatal shootings of Good and Pretti, called Miller an immigration hawk whose wings had been clipped.

“We should have doubled down and hit that community even harder,” he said, saying that to really address fraud, the administration needs to conduct mass deportations.

“You have to do large-scale, uniformed, hard immigration enforcement because that’s how you shut it down,” he said. “You have to put varsity squad there, whether it looks good or not.”

Fraud, he said, isn’t enough to sell Trump’s immigration promises to the base. Bovino argued Miller must do more in the last two years of Trump’s presidency.

“We’ve had the softer approach, the targeted enforcement … the very, ‘I’ll do a fraud case or two,’ gaslight the American public into thinking, OK, well we’re doing fraud cases’ when they’re really not,” he said. “And that’s what’s happening now in Minnesota and nationwide.”

The White House official said that “the administration has never wavered from it’s [sic] promise to arrest and deport illegal aliens.”

As the election neared, administration officials raced to right-wing television, social media and the Oval Office to tout their efforts to fight fraud. Top-level Cabinet members went to St. Cloud, Minnesota, days before Election Day to announce new anti-fraud measures.

“Let me be clear: This is still the beginning of our work in Minnesota,” said McDonald, the Miller point person in the DOJ. “We will be here for as long as it takes to punish the wrongdoers in Minnesota.”
entries.author: Natalie Alms, Jeff Stein, Paige Winfield Cunningham, Eric Katz, Jasmine Wright

entries.title: Democrats Are Ready to Pounce on Miller as Trump’s New Chief
entries.summary: Democrats quickly promised to make the Trump adviser a target for investigations, calling him “a dangerous xenophobe” and “a vile, hate-filled extremist.”
entries.content:
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee and its likely incoming chairman, had a message for the new White House chief of staff: “Lawyer up.”

After President Donald Trump said Friday that Stephen Miller would replace Susie Wiles, top Democrats pledged to make him a target of investigations.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said in a social media post that Trump “learned nothing from his historic defeat,” called Miller the architect of the administration’s most “inhumane policies” and said Democratic majorities would fight him at every step.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands” and wrote, “His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor.”

Jeffries told Trump to fire him the same day.

Several lawmakers characterized the shake-up as evidence the president had not learned from the election results or the GOP fallout after Democrats flipped both chambers.

“It appears he is doubling down on the disastrous policies and personnel that voters resoundingly rejected,” Sen. Jack Reed (D-Rhode Island) said in a statement. Reed called Miller an extremist and polarizing figure who has “dedicated his career trying to roll back the rights of every American.”

“Talk about absolute wrong lessons,” Shasti Conrad, a vice chair of the Democratic National Committee, told The Washington Sun.

In a statement, Garcia called Miller the “architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids” and said Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers had “kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families.”

“Lawyer up” is quickly becoming House Democrats’ go-to phrase. Those two words were the entirety of a statement Garcia released Tuesday night as news networks projected Democrats would flip the House. Friday was the first time he pointed those words at a specific person.

At a Wednesday news conference, though, he named a host of current and former administration officials as targets for investigations: Miller, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Noem’s former acting chief of staff, Corey Lewandowski.

“We're going to investigate the abuses,” Garcia said Wednesday. “We have a lot of questions for Stephen Miller. This is a man that created much of the harm that is being done.”

Miller is not the only focus. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth faces impeachment articles filed by members of both parties, and a House vote could come as early as next week.

The White House referred The Sun to Trump’s comments as he departed the White House for Florida on Friday.

"Stephen's been with me from the beginning,” Trump said. “He gets it very good politically, and he's a very good manager. He'll do a great job."

Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-New York), who chairs the Congressional Hispanic Caucus, said in a statement that Miller’s promotion was “a desperate and irresponsible cry for attention.”

Democrats on the House Homeland Security Committee, which oversees the portfolio Miller has run as homeland security adviser, called him “a vile, hate-filled extremist” and said Trump had rewarded him days after voters rejected his agenda.

Not every Democrat read the pick as a miscalculation.

Strategist Michael Ceraso called it a “brilliant move by the president” to put a man who understands the federal government, “whether legally or not, in a position to disrupt the Democrats.”

The question for Democrats, he told The Sun, is: “Can you focus on the issues, or will you get caught up in the personalities and the ways of those making the picks?”
entries.author: Ayah Ali-Ahmad
